Where it began

Tim Paine was born in Hobart on 8 December 1984 and grew up by the beach at Lauderdale, where the family driveway served as a pitch and the neighbours had a turf one of their own. He was a gifted Australian rules footballer as well, thought good enough for the AFL. Football ran in the family: his uncle, Robert Shaw, played and coached in the AFL.

Cricket won. At 16 he signed a rookie contract with Tasmania, then the youngest player ever contracted in Australian domestic cricket. He captained Australia at the 2004 Under-19 World Cup, and in October 2006 he made 215 against Western Australia at Perth for his first first-class hundred.

The player

Paine played 35 Tests for Australia between 2010 and 2021, scoring 1,534 runs at 32.64 with nine fifties, and taking 150 catches and 7 stumpings. His first Test, against Pakistan at Lord's in 2010, brought five catches and a stumping in a win, and it was the first time three Tasmanians had played together in an Australian Test side. Later that year he made 92 at Mohali, his best Test score.

After an injury and a long spell away from Tests, he was recalled for the 2017–18 Ashes, seven years on, and held 25 catches in the series. He captained Australia in 23 Tests, winning 11, losing 8 and drawing 4. In 2019 his side kept the Ashes in England, the first Australian team to do so since 2001, and the following home summer they won all five Tests against Pakistan and New Zealand.

What made him special

He was a neat, unfussy keeper, and the numbers show it. In December 2020 he reached 150 Test dismissals in his 33rd match, quicker than any keeper before him. With the bat he was an orthodox right-hander who played straight and used his wrists. He once tried to bat like Adam Gilchrist and Brad Haddin, then sensibly went back to the patient game that suited him.

The one thing that got away was a Test hundred. He came within eight runs of it at Mohali, and nine fifties suggest he knocked on the door often enough.

Away from the middle

He was part of the Australian side that won the 2009 Champions Trophy, and in 2010 he was Tasmania's Sports Personality of the Year. His playing days ended with Tasmania in March 2023, and his last match closed with a guard of honour. He then turned to coaching: as an assistant with the Adelaide Strikers from 2023, as head coach of the Prime Minister's XI against India in 2024, and in 2026 as head coach of Sialkot Stallionz, a new side in the Pakistan Super League.

And finally

As the 2017–18 season began he had been thinking about giving the game up, and someone talked him round. Before the year was out he was keeping wicket in an Ashes Test. Few cricketers have had a better reason to be glad they listened.
